LoloBuy size and variant checklist: how to choose the right listing option

A buyer-focused method for reading a seller’s size chart, option menu and product notes before you submit an order. It helps you record the choice you mean to buy; it cannot guarantee a seller’s stock, measurements or final product.

Editorial note: This independent guide is based on LoloBuy’s publicly available purchase and size-reference help materials, checked on 18 September 2026. Platform features, listing data and seller practices can change. Confirm the live order screen and listing before payment.

Why the option menu deserves more attention than the product photo

A product photo can make two options look almost identical. The option menu is where the actual purchase choice is usually made: colour, version, size, quantity, bundle, material or a seller-specific label. In agent-assisted shopping, an incomplete choice can travel through several steps before an item reaches the warehouse. That makes a two-minute check before submitting more valuable than trying to reconstruct the listing later.

LoloBuy’s public purchase guide says that supported listing information can be captured from certain marketplaces so that a buyer can select colour, size and quantity before adding an item to the cart or buying it. The same guide also describes a manual-order route when a listing cannot be captured. Treat both routes as a prompt to document the exact option, not as proof that the option text has been interpreted perfectly.

The narrow buyer question here is simple: how do I choose a size or variant on LoloBuy without relying on a guess? The answer is to save the seller’s own information, convert only the units you need, and create an order note that can later be checked against warehouse evidence. This is particularly useful for shoppers in the United States and Europe, where familiar S/M/L labels, shoe numbers and garment cuts may not map cleanly to a seller’s chart.

Start with the seller’s listing, not a generic conversion chart

Generic charts are a fallback, not the primary source. LoloBuy’s public size reference explicitly says that standards can vary between Taobao stores and recommends using body measurements such as bust, waist and hip when selecting a size. That is the sensible starting point for any listing: locate the seller’s chart and determine what the listed numbers actually measure.

First, identify whether the chart is for the body, the finished garment or both. A body chart might say that a range of chest measurements suits a size; a garment chart may show the chest width of the finished item. Those are different measurements. If the page does not say which it is, do not silently assume. Compare the item’s stated dimensions with a similar garment you own and can measure flat, then record the uncertainty in your order note.

Second, keep the original unit beside your conversion. One inch is 2.54 centimetres, but rounding can obscure a small difference. Write, for example, “seller chart: 112 cm chest; my comparison garment: 55 cm pit-to-pit flat” rather than only writing “large.” This gives you something meaningful to compare if a later photo shows a tag or a tape measurement.

Build a personal comparison set

Measure one or two garments that already fit the way you want. For a top, a practical set is chest width, shoulder width, length and sleeve length. For trousers, capture waist, rise, thigh, inseam and hem opening if those matter to you. Measure with the item laid flat unless the seller specifies another method. Use the same method every time; a number copied from a different measurement method can look precise while being useless.

For a looser or layered fit, write down the extra room you want rather than jumping a whole letter size. A chart may indicate a wider chest but a shorter length, or the opposite. The decision is therefore about the measurements that matter to the garment, not about winning a conversion-chart argument.

Read every option as a separate product specification

Before selecting a variant, expand the option menu and make a small “option map.” Copy the seller’s original label, then add a plain-English note of what you believe it means. Do this especially when an option combines colour, batch, material, size or set quantity in one line. “Black 2” may be a colourway, a version, a second batch, or a two-piece option; the listing photos and description must provide the context.

Use this five-part check for each selection:

1. Version: Is there a basic, upgraded, old, new, unbranded, lined, unlined, domestic or export-style variant? Do not substitute one version for another simply because the main image is shared.

2. Colour: Match the option label to the photo and description, not just to a thumbnail. Lighting and display settings can alter the perceived shade. A colour name may refer to a trim, a sole, a lining or a pack rather than the entire item.

3. Size: Tie the selected size to the seller’s measurement table. If the page has separate charts for men, women, youth or a particular cut, make sure you are using the correct one.

4. Quantity and bundle: Confirm whether “2” means two units, size 2, version 2, or a two-piece pack. If a price looks unexpectedly low, check whether it applies to one component rather than a complete set.

5. Included items: Look for notes about boxes, accessories, batteries, chargers, straps, inserts or replacement parts. A photo may show styling props that are not part of the purchase.

These checks do not invent information that the seller has not provided. They make gaps visible before money is committed. If an answer would change the choice, use the platform’s current order enquiry or manual-order fields where available and ask one precise question. “Which size should I get?” is hard to answer reliably. “Is 112 cm the finished chest measurement for size XL, measured flat around the garment?” is a question someone can verify.

Handle clothing, shoes and non-apparel differently

Clothing: keep labels secondary

For clothing, S/M/L labels are merely labels. The public LoloBuy size reference notes that garment tags can list figures such as height, waist, bust or body weight, and that manual measurements can differ by about 1–3 cm. That means a chart is useful evidence, but it is not a contractual fit guarantee. Choose with a range in mind and allow for the stated measurement tolerance. A buyer who needs an exact fit should avoid treating a single number as certainty.

Check whether the listing gives measurements for the body or for the garment; whether the fabric is described as stretch; and whether the item is intended to be oversized, cropped or slim. A “correct” chest measurement can still produce an unwanted fit if the shoulders, length or rise were not considered.

Shoes: use length before a country-size label

For shoes, use the seller’s stated foot or insole length when it is available. LoloBuy’s size guidance advises measuring feet and using the larger foot as the reference because feet are not perfectly symmetrical. It also cautions that Chinese shoe sizing does not express width. For a wider foot, compare the listing’s width information if present; if it is absent, do not turn a generic size conversion into a promise that the shoe will fit.

Save the selected shoe size, the listed length, whether the listing says foot length or insole length, and any width note. This is more useful than writing “US 9 equivalent,” because different sellers may use the same label for different measurements.

Electronics, accessories and sets: define compatibility

Non-apparel listings have variants too. A cable may differ by connector, length, plug or voltage; a watch strap by width; an accessory by left/right orientation; a cosmetic bundle by shade or quantity. Record the exact model or connector and the destination-relevant detail such as plug type or voltage. Do not assume an adapter, battery, branded box or pictured accessory is included unless the option text or description says so.

Create an order note that can survive the warehouse stage

A good note is short enough to be read, but specific enough to test. Use this template before you submit:

Item: seller title and link
Selected option: original option label plus your plain-English description
Size basis: seller chart measurement and your comparison measurement
Quantity: number of complete units or set contents
Must match: two or three observable details such as size tag, connector, colourway or component count
Stop and ask: the mismatch that would change your decision

For example: “Size XL / blue-grey version; seller chart says 112 cm chest; compare with 55 cm flat chest garment; one complete jacket; must match XL tag, blue-grey outer shell and included belt; ask if the chart uses garment circumference or body measurement.” This is better than “XL please.” It allows you to assess a warehouse photo against a decision made before you saw it.

LoloBuy’s purchase guide says that buyers can view quality-control photos after an item arrives at the warehouse. Use that stage to check identity and obvious visible details against your note. It does not prove fit, authenticity, durability or compliance with local rules, and a photo cannot resolve a missing chart. It can, however, reveal a plainly different tag, colour, component or quantity early enough to use the platform’s current support options.

Know when to pause rather than force a selection

Pause the order if the listing has no chart for a size-critical item, if options use terms you cannot distinguish, if the price and set contents do not add up, or if photos conflict with the selected label. The right outcome is sometimes not an immediate purchase; it is a question, a different listing or no order. A buying agent can purchase a chosen listing, but it cannot make unclear seller data reliable after the fact.

Also separate a factual mismatch from a preference change. A different selected colour, missing component or wrong size tag can be checked against the saved option. Deciding that a properly selected cut is not flattering is different. Current return, exchange and refund availability can depend on the seller, item condition and time limits, so review the live platform guidance before relying on any remedy.

Conclusion: save the evidence that defines your choice

The practical LoloBuy size and variant checklist is not complicated: use the seller’s own measurements first; preserve original option labels; verify version, colour, size, quantity and included parts; and turn the final choice into a short note. Then use warehouse-stage evidence to check the few details that matter most. This approach will not eliminate seller, sizing or fulfilment risk, but it gives you a clear record of what you selected and why.
